sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Robot-use Agents (RUAs) have shown promising zero-shot manipulation capabilities, but reliance on frontier, proprietary models limits research into further training. To democratize RUA research, we introduce uni-robot-agent, a unified harness for competitive open-weight robot use that supports further training. Without privileged inputs, an out-of-the-box Qwen3.8-Flash-Next achieves a RoboDojo Score of 31.39, surpassing the published GPT-6 Astra-RoboProbe result of 28.97 and many VLA/WAM baselines, and performs competitively on 19 real-world tasks. Our analysis across model generations, families, and sizes links effective robot use to four general capabilities, suggesting that future RUA training should develop them jointly.

F.2 Preparing Reorientation During Transport . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 25 26 28 28 29 32 32 33 34 35 3 1. Introduction Recent breakthroughs in frontier foundation models (e.g., GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI, 2026b), Opus 5.5 (Anthropic, 2026)) have shown surprising zero-shot performance in robotic manipulation, highlighting robot-use agents (RUAs) (Isola, 2026) as promising approach for robotics (Chen et al., 2026b; Qu et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026b). This approach effectively transfers the models generic problem-solving capabilities, such as task decomposition and failure recovery, which are hard to learn from limited robotics data alone, yet extremely useful for robotics (Chu et al., 2026; Isola, 2026; Jia et al., 2026). However, because these frontier foundation models are proprietary, research on RUAs has been limited to using the models as-is, such as harness design (Li et al., 2026; Si et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026b). Without access to their weights, researchers cannot directly explore how further training of these models can advance RUA capabilities. Moreover, API dependence makes large-scale interaction costly (OpenAI, 2026b) and restricts model-level optimization, such as efficient caching, despite inference speed being major bottleneck for RUA (Isola, 2026). The main challenge in adapting open-weight models for robot use is the capability gap between open-weight and closed-weight foundation models. Robot use demands strong spatial understanding and agentic capabilities, which existing open-weight models often lack. Consequently, prior work has focused on ad-hoc improvements, including leveraging privileged information such as ground-truth simulator states or oracle task-success feedback (Fu et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026c), or incorporating task-specific skills (Lu et al., 2026). Before attributing these limitations to the models themselves and pursuing ad-hoc improvements, we argue that we must first establish generalizable and effective robot-use harness to systematically understand and maximize their existing capabilities, laying the foundation for future RUA training. In this paper, we take first step toward democratizing robot-use agent research by laying this foundation for both competitive open-weight agents and future robot-specific training. We introduce uni-robot-agent, general-purpose RUA harness. It provides Unified tool interfaces and feedback formats across models, embodiments, tasks, and environments, supporting joint training on simulation and real-world interaction data. For future large-scale training, we emphasize Efficiency by overlapping model reasoning with tool execution to accelerate interaction, and Modularity through interchangeable agent runtimes, tools, and robot backends. Together, these designs provide scalable, extensible foundation for RUA research. The proposed uni-robot-agent enables competitive manipulation performance with openweight models, including Qwen and DeepSeek, in both simulation and physical environments. key finding is that well-structured information, such as camera calibration and robot descriptions, together with reliable tool interfaces that provide informative feedback, are sufficient for effective robot use. As result, without privileged inputs, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next with uni-robotagent achieves Score of 31.39, surpassing GPT-6 Astras result (28.97) on RoboDojo (Chen et al., 2026a) from the RoboDojo team (Zhang et al., 2026a). To the best of our knowledge, this is the first system to outperform closed-weight foundation models on RoboDojo using open-weight models, without privileged informations or distillation from those closed-weight models. In real-world experiments on 19 tabletop manipulation tasks, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next with uni-robot-agent achieves Score of 49.50, outperforming Dream-1 (35.50; Dream Labs, 2026) and matching fine-tuned 𝜋0.5 (47.75; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025). Having established the competitiveness of open-weight RUAs, we further compare models across generations, families, and sizes to investigate the capabilities underlying robot use. Trajectory analysis reveals four common failure patterns involving visual understanding, spatial 4 Figure 2 Five logical layers of uni-robot-agent. Requests flow from agent runtimes through orchestration and shared tools to domain services and native backends. Context policies and concrete backends are replaceable components; arrows summarize logical interactions rather than individual network connections. grounding, geometric coding, and embodied reasoning. Based on these findings, we posit that current robot-use capability emerges from combination of these general-purpose capabilities and identify them as key areas for improvement in future RUA training. Finally, we provide an analysis of the effect of privileged information, cost, and execution efficiency. 2. uni-robot-agent: Unified and Modular Harness In this section, we introduce the key mechanisms of uni-robot-agent. We describe how the harness connects diverse agents, robot environments, and embodiments through shared tools and supports interaction based on information only available in real-world deployments. 2.1. System Overview uni-robot-agent connects different agent runtimes to shared toolkit for simulation and physical robots. The agent selects operations using task instructions and observations, while the harness executes them and returns feedback. We organize this interaction around four principles: Unified. Shared tools give operations and feedback common meaning across environments, with adapters handling native APIs (Section 2.2). The resulting interaction records can also be combined for subsequent training. Efficient. Reasoning should overlap physical execution, while operations that share resource retain their required order (Section 2.3). Realistic. Agents and tools should rely on information available in physical deployments, without simulator-provided depth or task-verifier feedback (Section 2.4). Modular. Explicit interfaces should allow researchers to replace runtimes, tools, and perception models independently. We introduce this architecture below. These principles guide how we organize the system, but reliable interaction also requires care in how observations, actions, and feedback are handled. We first describe the architecture, then examine these practical design choices in Section 2.5. Modular Architecture. tool call passes through five layers with explicit interfaces (Figure 2). The agent layer manages model interaction and context, passing tool requests to the orchestration layer for scheduling and dispatch. The tool layer implements shared robot operations and accesses environment, perception, and action-model capabilities through the service layer, which manages their runtime resources. The backend layer supplies the concrete simulator, robot, and model implementations used by these services. Results return through these interfaces to the agent, completing the interaction. 2.2. Unified Interaction Interface Moving gripper to target pose should mean the same thing in simulation and on physical robot, even when their control APIs differ. We give agents shared set of tools for motion, perception, skills, and episode control, with common arguments, units, and feedback formats. Environment descriptions identify the available arms, cameras, and optional capabilities. This lets the agent use familiar operations while accounting for the robot and sensors available in each environment. Figure 3 Tool reuse across environments. Shared tools avoid 𝑁 𝑀 implementations. 𝑇: tool; 𝐴: adapter; 𝐸: environment. To make these operations work across environments, shared tools access observations, robot state, and primitive actions through common interface implemented by environment adapters. For example, the shared move tool generates intermediate targets and monitors progress; the adapter translates those targets into native commands and returns the resulting state. Adding an environment therefore requires an adapter and its configuration rather than separate implementation of every tool. As Figure 3 illustrates, 𝑁 tools can share their logic across 𝑀 adapters, avoiding 𝑁 𝑀 toolenvironment implementations. The common request and feedback formats also make the experience collected across environments easier to combine for subsequent training. 6 2.3. Efficient Execution The orchestration layer determines how agent interaction proceeds while tools are running. Waiting for every movement to finish delays reasoning that could proceed independently, yet successive movements may still need to execute in order. We combine background tool calls with resource-aware scheduling to satisfy both requirements, forming pipeline between agent reasoning and tool execution. Two Levels of Concurrency. The agent need not wait for every tool, but its next call may still need to wait for resource: Between agent and tools. background call returns job handle, allowing the agent to continue independent reasoning and retrieve the result later; an immediate call waits for completion. Decisions that depend on the result must still wait. Among tool calls. Calls sharing an exclusive resource execute in submission order; parallel calls run outside that queue. Two move calls on the same resource therefore run sequentially, while reading an existing snapshot can overlap movement. Two-Stage Pipelining. These mechanisms enable two-stage pipeline comprising agent reasoning and tool execution (Figure 4). The agent can submit successive calls while previously submitted calls execute in resource order. Reasoning and execution thus overlap even when the tools themselves execute sequentially. When observations or execution feedback require change of plan, the agent can use flush_queue to cancel calls that have not started for specified resource. Where supported, single model response can submit multiple tool requests, and batched wait can retrieve multiple results. 2.4. Interaction Without Privileged Inputs Figure 4 Serial interaction and pipelining. Reasoning (𝑅) overlaps sequential tools (𝑇); 𝑇2 queues while 𝑇1 runs. Solid/dashed arrows show submissions/results; shading marks overlap. Timings are schematic. Efficient execution alone does not ensure that simulation performance carries over to physical robots: the information supporting each action also matters. Existing systems provide depthbased geometry and completion checks (Li et al., 2026), or construct object models to maintain virtual scene (Wang et al., 2026). In physical settings, depth measurements can vary or be missing even in static scene, and simulator task-verifier feedback is unavailable. These differences motivate testing whether agents can infer spatial relationships and assess progress from more limited observations. 2.5. Key Design Choices Effective robot use requires careful design of how observations reach the agent, how commands are executed, and how outcomes inform subsequent decisions. We introduce six practical design 7 Figure 5 Key design choices. Each column pairs two designs for physical consistency, action precision, or context management. choices spanning observation and execution consistency, coordinated motion control, progress monitoring, actionable feedback, and visual context management. Keeping Observations and State Consistent. When robot moves after an image is captured, interpreting selected pixel using newer camera pose mixes two physical states. We bind images, camera calibration, and robot state to an immutable snapshot and use that snapshot for localization (Figure 5a). The agent and tools thus work from the same recorded state. Preventing Repeated Actions After Communication Failures. The agent must also know which actions have occurred: missing reply may mean lost feedback, so retrying could repeat physical action. We record request identities and execution status to reject duplicates (Figure 5b). If completion is uncertain, further actions are blocked while the session attempts to recover the execution record; unresolved requests remain explicitly marked as uncertain. Coordinating Motion and Gripper Control. Separate movement and gripper commands prevent the agent from adjusting the opening during movement. Our move tool accepts target pose and an optional gripper opening together, allowing the arm and gripper to act simultaneously (Figure 5c). Detecting When Motion Should Stop. During execution, fixed step count may stop motion too early or waste steps on an unreachable target. Our move tool generates intermediate targets 8 from measured poses and checks progress after each step (Figure 5d). This lets the tool adjust motion locally, stop on arrival, and return control when motion stalls or reaches an execution limit. Appendix gives the algorithm and stopping criteria. Making Action Outcomes Diagnosable. Reaching target pose does not establish that an object was grasped or placed successfully. We return numerical motion feedback, including pose errors and stopping reasons, alongside images of the outcome (Figure 5e). The numbers distinguish small residual error from rejected or stalled motion; the images show the effect on the object. Together, they help the agent decide whether to refine the motion or change its manipulation strategy. Managing Growing Visual Histories. This feedback accumulates, but old images may lose relevance while task instructions and action records remain useful. Our sliding window replaces old images with text placeholders, preserving recent images and the surrounding text (Figure 5f). We evict images in batches to keep the prompt prefix stable between evictions and support cache reuse. If the context still exceeds budget, we compact the history with the same model that we use for the policy, using the compaction prompt of the codex CLI (OpenAI, 2026a). 3. Can Open Models Use Robots in Simulation and the Real World? Effective robot use has largely been the preserve of frontier, closed-source models. In this work, however, we show that open-weight models can also achieve competitive performance in simulation and on physical robots. In particular, on RoboDojo, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next surpasses most fine-tuned VLA and WAM baselines in zero-shot setting without privileged information, and also the GPT-6 Astras result reported by the RoboDojo team. On real robots, less-explored setting in prior works, open-weight models also achieve competitive performance, showing their real-world applicability. These results highlight the viability of open-source robot-use agents and the importance of properly designed harness for supporting these models. 3.1. Simulation Evaluation 3.1.1. Setup We evaluate 42 RoboDojo (Chen et al., 2026a) tasks spanning generalization, memory, precision, long-horizon execution, and open-vocabulary instruction following. We report the success rate and the score (incorporating partial success, scaled to 0100) following the RoboDojos evaluation protocol. The result is averaged over three seeds with two layouts (six episodes per task, 252 episodes in total). The 12 generalization tasks pair equally weight standard and randomized layouts per seed to test robustness to object and scene changes. Following the official protocol, we average the result of each tasks within the dimension, and average those results over the five dimensions. No Privileged Inputs. Our simulation uses the inputs of realistic robotics applications, providing only RGB images and camera calibration, robot proprioception and descriptions, and task instructions. We do not allow access to ground-truth depth from simulators, CAD assets of the object, hidden scene annotations, task-verifier feedback, and external web access. To contextualize open-weight model performance, we compare against official Astra RoboProbe (Zhang et al., 2026a) results and representative VLA and WAM baselines from the RoboDojo leaderboard (RoboDojo Team, 2026). To compare the contribution of the harness, we compare Qwen3.8-Flash-Next across uni-robot-agent, GAP (Hybrid) (Su et al., 2026), RoboProbe, and RPent (Zhang et al., 2026c). Baseline configurations are detailed in Appendix A. 3.1.2. Results and Analysis As shown in Table 1, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next with uni-robot-agent achieves 25.00% SR and 31.39 Score, surpassing listed VLA/WAM baselines and GPT-6 Astra with RoboProbe (22.48% SR, 28.97 Score), despite being an open-weight model. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash also outperforms the VLA/WAM baselines (21.39% SR, 27.11 Score). Moreover, switching to other harnesses results in substantially degrades the performance (loss of 8.89% SR and 10.38 Score on the strongest baseline GAP). Together, these results demonstrate competitive robot use across two open-weight families and the importance of our harness on this performance. Both open-weight or closed-source RUAs tend to achieve higher scores on memory and open-vocabulary tasks than the VLA and WAM baselines. On long-horizon tasks, however, Qwen and DeepSeek perform worse than Xiaomi-Robotics-1 and OpenWAM-𝛼. sections.title: Unseen tasks
sections.content: Total 3.2. Real-World Evaluation 3.2.1. Setup We design an in-house benchmark with 19 tasks across five equally weighted dimensions: spatial understanding, object generalization, instruction following, compositional generalization, and unseen tasks. We evaluate Qwen3.8-Flash-Next and GPT-6 Astra with uni-robot-agent, alongside Dream-1 (Dream Labs, 2026) in zero-shot setting, while 𝜋0.5 (Physical Intelligence et al., 2025) is fine-tuned on 10 hours of demonstrations per task. All methods use the same dual-arm platform. We note that our agents additionally receive depth from Intel RealSense D405 cameras, while 𝜋0.5 and Dream-1 use RGB only. Appendix provides the task catalogue, scoring protocol, hardware, and baseline details. 3.2.2. Results and Analysis As shown in Table 2, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next with uni-robot-agent matches the performance of fine-tuned 𝜋0.5, and outperforms zero-shot Dream-1 in real world experiments. When applied to GPT-6 Astra, it outperforms other baselines with large margin. Generally, RUAs perform better on compositional tasks and unseen tasks, while VLA/WAMs performing well on object generalization tasks. These results show that uni-robot-agent can be also applied to real world applications. Please refer to Table 4 for detailed per-task results. 4. What Capabilities Enable Robot-Use Agents? The results in Section 3 establish the feasibility of robot use with open-weight models, but leave an important question: what enables these models to work? To investigate this, we examine three comparisons. First, we revisit earlier model generations, including Qwen3.53.7 and GPT-5.6. Second, we compare recent models from different families, including Qwen, DeepSeek, GLM, and GPT. Third, we examine Qwen models of different sizes within the same generation. 4.1. Setup We evaluate the additional models on RoboDojos 42 tasks and report SR and Score using the same aggregation as Section 3. We reuse the Section 3 results for Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, and GPT-6 Astra. The additional evaluations use one seed and one layout. 11 4.2. Performance Across Generations, Families, and Model Sizes Figure 6 Robot-use performance across model generations, families, and sizes. Success rate (top) and Score (bottom) on RoboDojo with uni-robot-agent. Robot use is neither exclusive to frontier models nor unique to the latest generation: GPT-5.6 Sol already achieves nontrivial performance, while Qwen3.8-27B succeeds where larger, earlier Qwen models fail. Shading indicates closed-source models. Robot use predates the latest model generation. Figure 6 shows that GPT-5.6 Sol already achieves nontrivial 19.17% SR and 24.04 Score, while GPT-6.1 Sol reaches 37.50% SR and 45.63 Score. Thus, the latest generation substantially improves robot-use performance, but these capabilities were already present in earlier models. The pattern differs across model families. However, among the models evaluated, only the GPT series demonstrates successful robot use in generations preceding the latest one. For Qwen, verified task success is observed only in the 3.8 generation: Qwen3.53.7 Flash, Qwen3.63.7 Plus, and Qwen3.5-122B record zero SR, whereas Qwen3.8-27B and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next achieve 8.06% and 25.00%, respectively. More importantly, recent model generation does not by itself guarantee task success: GLM-5.3 Flash shows 0% success rate as older Qwen models. Model size matters less than training distribution. Within Qwen3.8, Flash-Next (125B) achieves higher SR and Score than the 27B model. Across generations, however, Qwen3.8-27B completes tasks while all earlier Qwen models evaluated, including Qwen3.5-122B, Qwen3.7 Plus (> 150B parameters), and Qwen3.6 Plus (> 150B parameters), record zero SR. We posit that training distributions differ substantially across generations and that these differences matter more for robot use than model size alone. Taken together, these results suggest that robot use is neither exclusive to frontier models nor capability that emerged uniformly with the latest generation. Earlier GPT models already Figure 7 Four capabilities associated with effective robot use. Correlation between each models RoboDojo Score and its errors in (a) general visual understanding, (b) spatial grounding, (c) coding in geometry, and (d) embodied reasoning. Lower error rates across these dimensions are associated with higher task performance, suggesting that effective robot use draws on combination of these capabilities achieve nontrivial performance, while Qwen3.8-27B succeeds where larger, earlier Qwen models fail. Rather than model size or recency alone, these contrasting trajectories point to differences in the underlying capabilities (i.e. training distribution) developed across model families and generations. We next examine failure modes to identify which capabilities distinguish successful robot use from failure. 4.3. Four Major Failure Modes Our trajectory analysis identifies four major failure types: general visual understanding, such as misinterpreting objects or action outcomes; fine-grained pointing and spatial grounding, such as selecting inconsistent corresponding points across views; localization and pose computation code, involving errors in geometric calculations, coordinate transformations, or orientation construction; and embodied reasoning, such as proposing physically inappropriate grasp poses. Figure 7 summarizes these four failure types across thirteen models. 13 General visual understanding. Perhaps the most straightforward reason for failures in earlier Qwen Flash and Plus models is basic visual misunderstanding. Such errors, including mistaking zero for nine or inverted cups for upright ones, occur in 12.223.8% of trials. In contrast, these kinds of errors occur in 3.2% of Qwen3.8-27B trials and none of the trials from more performant models such as Qwen3.8-Flash or GPT-5.6 Sol. These observations suggest that general visual understanding is closely associated with its performance. Spatial grounding. In addition to coarse scene understanding, we find that models struggle to pinpoint the same physical feature across camera views. Selecting inconsistent pixels for the same feature leads to large reprojection errors, causing the triangulation tool to reject the result. We therefore use the fraction of calls rejected for this reason to measure difficulty in pinpointing corresponding features. Task performance tends to be negatively associated with this failure rate: Qwen3.8-Flash and DeepSeek have lower failure rates than models with zero task success, including Qwen3.53.7 Flash and Qwen3.7 Plus. GPT-6.1 Sol achieves the lowest spatial-grounding failure rate among the evaluated models (31.5%), but this substantial remaining error rate highlights precise spatial grounding as common challenge for further improvement (Figure 7b). Coding in geometry Coding skill is also closely correlated with task performance, as illustrated by geometry computations involving coordinate transformations and orientations. Earlier Qwen models frequently reverse coordinate transforms or mix quaternion conventions, with such errors affecting 47.381.8% of executed calculations across the earlier Flash and Plus cohorts. In contrast, the error rates are 8.2% for Qwen3.8-Flash, 1.5% for DeepSeek, and 0.7% for GPT-5.6 Sol, with no errors in GPT-6.1 Sols calculations. The pattern suggests that reliable robot-specific computation is another capability associated with effective robot use (Figure 7c). Embodied reasoning. Beyond perceiving and computing target pose, robot use requires embodied reasoning to propose appropriate interactions, including grasp poses. Because this broad capability is difficult to measure, we restrict our analysis to pick-and-place and use GPT-6 Astra to assess whether proposed grasp poses are physically reasonable. We report the rate at which the model proposed unnatural or infeasible grasping poses and failed to correct them in these tasks (Figure 7d). To our surprise, even recent models can lack this capability: GLM repeatedly fails to reorient its wrist for grasping, contributing to many unsuccessful trials and 26.2% error rate. Such errors are less frequent in newer Qwen and GPT models, which more often select appropriate grasp orientations. However, grasp-pose proposal is only one instance of embodied reasoning. GPT-6 Astra still struggles with other skills, including bimanual coordination, where inappropriate interaction plans limit performance. Embodied reasoning therefore appears to improve across model generations, but remains substantial bottleneck beyond this narrow grasping analysis. In conclusion, these failure patterns suggest that effective robot use draws on combination of visual understanding, spatial grounding, geometric coding, and embodied reasoning, rather than single robot-specific capability. This suggests that general model capabilities provide substantial foundation for robot use. We therefore argue that future RUA training should develop these capabilities jointly for example, by using robot data to construct training tasks targeting each capability rather than focusing solely on fitting action outputs. 14 Figure 8 Robot-use performance and general model capabilities. Each point denotes model, with benchmark performance on the horizontal axis and RoboDojo Score on the vertical axis. Q35Q38 denote Qwen Flash generations; DS denotes DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017. Dashed lines show linear fits; Pearson correlations are computed across the six models. 4.4. Relationship to General Model Capabilities Having identified four key capabilities underlying effective robot use through failure analysis, we next ask: To what extent can these capabilities be captured by existing foundation-model benchmarks? To investigate this, we compare RoboDojo performance with scores on four corresponding benchmarks: MMMU-Pro (Yue et al., 2024) for general visual understanding, ERQA (Gemini Robotics Team et al., 2025) for embodied reasoning, ScreenSpot-Pro (Li et al., 2025) for spatial grounding, and LiveCodeBench v6 (Jain et al., 2024) for code generation (Figure 8). We observe positive correlations across all four benchmarks, with particularly strong correlations for embodied reasoning and general visual understanding, while spatial grounding exhibits weaker correlation, potentially because ScreenSpot-Pro evaluates 2D screen-based grounding rather than the 3D spatial grounding required for robotic manipulation. These findings further support the role of general-purpose model capabilities in robot use, suggesting that advances in these capabilities may translate into improved robotic performance. 5. Analysis on Privileged Information As discussed in Section 2.4, privileged inputs such as precise simulator-provided depth and oracle task-success feedback can assist robot interaction. Although uni-robot-agent operates without these inputs, it remains important to understand how much they affect robot-use performance. We first challenge whether depth, commonly used source of geometric information, Figure 9 Robot use with less geometric information. Recorded progress through 771 tool calls and final score across 42 tasks, with skills enabled. is necessary for better performance (RQ1). Second, since skill libraries can encode privileged information or task-specific solutions, we ablate our skill library to test whether performance depends on such leak of privileged information (RQ2). 5.1. RQ1: How Does Depth Affect Robot Use? We compare three levels of geometric information for depth: RGB images with depth and camera parameters, RGB images with camera parameters, and only RGB images. With depth and camera parameters, agent can infer 3D coordinates directly from the pixel. Having only camera parameters requires the agent to find the pixel of corresponding points in multiple cameras. Without either, the agents should infer the coordinates through spatial relationships of the objects in the image. We evaluate GPT-6 Astra and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on the same 42 benchmark tasks. The evaluation uses three seeds and two layouts per task for Qwen and one seed and one layout per task for Astra due to limited evaluation costs. Without depth, agents can still recover object positions with the camera parameters by triangulating the corresponding points across views. Evidently, Astras score changes from 55.83 to 55.04, and Qwens score changes from 35.89 to 31.39, retaining 98.6% and 87.5% of their depth-enabled scores, respectively (Figures 9a and 9b), reflecting minimal loss in performance, especially with stronger model capabilities. The cases in Appendix further shows that Qwen writes and executes its own geometry code to infer 3D coordinates, such as triangulating object positions across views and testing candidate table heights with the images. Without camera parameters (only RGB images), where agents must infer 3D positions from abstract spatial relationships, Qwens performance shows sharp drop to 9.13, while Astra shows moderate decrease on its performance to 31.29 (Figure 9c). In conclusion, we find that privileged depth information is not necessary for achieving strong robot-use performance as long as camera parameters are available. In fact, as model capabilities improve, models can more effectively infer 3D spatial relationships from visual observations, thereby benefiting less from such privileged inputs. 16 Figure 10 Effect of skill guidance on task performance. Qwen3.8-Flash-Next with uni-robot-agent, evaluated with and without skills. Error bars indicate approximate 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. 5.2. RQ2: Is skill library important for uni-robot-agent? Task-specific skill libraries may encode privileged information or predefined solutions that simplify robot tasks. We therefore examine whether the performance of uni-robot-agent depends on the knowledge provided by its skill library. Using Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, we disable access to the robot skill library and skill writing (we retain task instructions, environment descriptions, and standard robot tools). Figure 10 shows small aggregate performance gap between configurations with and without robot skills. The no-skill configuration reaches 30.31 score and 24.58% SR, retaining 96.6% of the skill-enabled score (31.39), with an SR gap of only 0.42 percentage points. These results show that uni-robot-agent maintains comparable performance without the skill library. The harness supports reusable skills, but its robot-use performance does not depend on the task-specific knowledge they provide. 6. Analysis on Cost and Speed In this section, we focus on the time and resources required for uni-robot-agent across different models, and show that pipelining of uni-robot-agent substantially improves the execution time. 6.1. Token Usage and API Cost robot-use agent may spend many model calls and reasoning for locating objects, testing grasp, or recovering from an unsuccessful action. We analyze the results from Section 3.1, examining how task performance relates to token usage, API cost, and progress during execution across different models. Reference API prices are provided in Appendix C. 17 Figure 11 Model-level resourceperformance trade-offs. Astra, Qwen, and DeepSeek each use 252 episodes. Bars show score and mean resource usage per episode. Figure 12 Task progress over token usage and time. score is aggregated from recorded intermediate outcomes for the same model cohorts as Figure 11. Curves retain each episodes latest observed score. Figure 11 shows that Qwen offers favorable trade-off between the performance and the cost, reaching 31.39 score at $1.09 per episode. Astra achieves the highest score (51.90), but costs nearly 20x more ($21.29 per episode). This substantial difference of each models cost highlights the value of advancing open-weight models for affordable robot-use agents. Figure 12 shows that each models need substantially different amount of tokens to make progress. To reach score of 25, Astra requires 7.4M tokens per episode, which is less than 23.5M for Qwen and 49.9M for DeepSeek. This trend also persists in terms of the wall-clock time, where Astra reaches score of 25 after 42.6 minutes, while Qwen and DeepSeek take 95.5 and 99.2 minutes, respectively. 18 Figure 13 Modelaction overlap in pipelined execution. Blue and green bars show model requests and physical actions; shading marks overlap. Percentages indicate the fraction of action time overlapping model requests. Each panel starts at the first action and uses its own time range. 6.2. Execution Efficiency The pipeline introduced in Section 2.3 allows model interaction to continue while physical actions is being executed. We select five tasks and compare pipelined and serial execution of uni-robot-agent using GPT-6 Astra with medium reasoning effort. Each task is evaluated once per configuration with the same seed and layout. We measure episode duration excluding simulator initialization and the overlap between model requests and physical tool execution. Episode Duration. As shown in Figure 14, the pipelined runs have shorter episode durations on all five tasks, with observed reductions ranging from 4.8% to 73.7% relative to serial execution. For example, swap_T takes 12.5 minutes with pipelining versus 34.7 minutes with serial execution, while press_by_number takes 13.7 versus 25.0 minutes. Execution Overlap. We measure the fraction of physical execution time that overlaps with model request. As shown in Figure 13, it ranges from 84.5% to 93.8% in the pipelined episodes and is zero in all five serial episodes, showing that most of the physical execution time is pipelined with the model inference. Appendix shows additional qualitative case studies. 19 Figure 14 Episode duration on five selected tasks. Pipelined and serial execution are compared using one episode per configuration and task, excluding simulator initialization. 7. Related Work Vision-Language-Action and World-Action Models. Vision-language-action (VLA) models extend robot policies beyond task-specific demonstrations by transferring pretrained visuallanguage representations and learning from diverse robot data (Brohan et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024). Training on heterogeneous sources has further improved generalization: 𝜋0.5 performs manipulation in previously unseen environments by combining robot experience with semantic supervision and web data (Physical Intelligence et al., 2025). World-action models (WAMs) explore complementary route through predictive modeling. Joint video and action generation enables DreamZero to generalize to unseen tasks and environments (Ye et al., 2026), while Cosmos Policy uses predicted future states and values to support test-time planning (Kim et al., 2026). These advances broaden where learned policies can operate and what behaviors they can perform. Reliable use of past observations and recovery from failures over extended interactions nevertheless remain important areas for further investigation. Tool-Using Agents for Robot Control. Tool use allows language models to organize decisions around observations and feedback. In computer environments, agents operate graphical interfaces through repeated observation and action, combining visual grounding with planning and context management (Agashe et al., 2025; Anthropic, 2024; Wang et al., 2025). Robotics research has explored related ideas through skill selection and programmatic composition of perception and control APIs (Ahn et al., 2022; Liang et al., 2022). Environment feedback enables replanning (Huang et al., 2022), while spatial representations connect language instructions to physical motion (Huang et al., 2023). Together, these studies establish ways for general-purpose models to direct interaction through tools. In robotics, this interaction must also account for world that changes while actions are running, making the coordination of observation, reasoning, and execution central concern. Robot-Use Agents and Harnesses. Recent studies show that general-purpose multimodal models can operate robots through tools without task-specific robot training (Isola, 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a). This has prompted efforts to design the harness through which model observes the scene, issues actions, and receives feedback. RoboDawn and Robo-Harness K1 provide 20 motion and geometric perception tools (Guo et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026), while OpenRUA gives coding agents access to native ROS 2 interfaces through terminal (Chu et al., 2026). Beyond these interfaces, Harness VLA and GAP investigate how agents can guide learned policies through memory-based planning and corrections to policy-generated actions (Su et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026c). ORA also demonstrates robot use with open-weight models, combining robot tools with environment information and context management (Yang et al., 2026). As robot use expands to more models and environments, reusing these components becomes an important system-design question. We develop uni-robot-agent around this need, separating shared robot tools from model runtimes and environment adapters so that changing one does not require rebuilding the others. We also coordinate tool execution and feedback to let agents continue reasoning while physical actions are underway. 8. Conclusion We presented uni-robot-agent, unified and modular harness with efficient execution and reliable tools for robot-use agents. Evaluations demonstrate strong performance with GPT-6 Astra in both simulation and real-world manipulation. More importantly, our results show that an open-weight model can also achieve strong robot-use performance: Qwen3.8-FlashNext reaches RoboDojo Score of 31.39, exceeding the published AstraRoboProbe result of 28.97. These findings support further investigation of open-weight models that can be deployed locally and adapted through training on robot experience. Precise manipulation and reliable long-horizon execution remain challenges in our evaluations. By providing shared interaction interfaces, replaceable components, and structured execution feedback, uni-robot-agent offers unified foundation for collecting robot interaction data, developing training methods, and evaluating their effects on agent behavior and task performance.

We compare agent harnesses using Qwen3.8-Flash-Next as the planner. GPT-as-Policy (GAP) (Su et al., 2026) uses its hybrid configuration with 𝜋0.5; RoboProbe (Zhang et al., 2026a) and RPent (Zhang et al., 2026c) use their default configurations. Table 1 also includes the published AstraRoboProbe results and representative vision-language-action (VLA) and world-action models (WAM) from the RoboDojo leaderboard (RoboDojo Team, 2026). Reasoning effort. We use medium reasoning effort for GPT-6 Astra, high for both GPT-5.6 Sol and GPT-6.1 Sol, xhigh for all Qwen-series Models, and max for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. B. Real Eval Benchmark Details Real Eval evaluates tabletop manipulation on dual-arm gripper platform through five capability dimensions: spatial understanding, object generalization, instruction following, compositional generalization, and unseen tasks. Its test catalogue contains 19 evaluation entries, with 20 points allocated to each dimension and 100 points in total. An evaluation entry specifies an operation together with the variation being tested: bowl stacking, for example, appears both as an object-generalization test and as direction-following test. The catalogue therefore distinguishes changes in objects, language, and task structure even when they share manipulation primitive. Table 3 gives the complete test catalogue and its scoring criteria. B.1. Hardware and Baselines All methods run on an ARX AC one dual-arm platform with two X5 arms and three Intel RealSense D405 cameras, comprising head view and wrist view on each arm. We evaluate uni-robot-agent with GPT-6 Astra and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next as planners and compare both configurations with 𝜋0.5 (Physical Intelligence et al., 2025), fine-tuned on demonstrations from the same platform. We also include Dream-1 (Dream Labs, 2026), world action model evaluated zero-shot through its public API (dreamlabs/dream-1-beta). In the real-world evaluation, uni-robot-agent additionally uses the D405 depth stream, whereas 𝜋0.5 and Dream-1 natively consume only RGB images. B.2. Training Task Catalogue and Collection Protocol The accompanying training catalogue lists 30 task templates and 1,550 trajectories: 27 templates specify 50 trajectories each, while bag zipping, coin insertion, and tissue extraction specify 100, 80, and 20, respectively. The templates span stacking and sorting, object transfer and handover, container loading, cloth manipulation, surface wiping, and operation of buttons, switches, drawers, and microwave door. Collection protocols vary object placement, material, color, container arrangement, and table appearance at task-specific intervals. For example, paper-cup stacking uses four to six inverted cups at different positions, changes cup material every five trajectories, and changes the table mat every ten. Test-tube transfer uses three to four tubes of different sizes and reverses the transfer direction every five trajectories. Cloth folding includes two folds per trajectory, changes cloth orientation every three trajectories, and changes the cloth every six. These collection settings establish the reference operations and variations against which the test catalogue defines new objects, instructions, and action combinations. The catalogue is collected to fine-tune end-to-end embodied policies such as 𝜋0.5, whereas uni-robot-agent does not use any of these demonstrations; for uni-robot-agent, every entry is therefore evaluated zero-shot, and the five dimensions characterize the type of variation that each entry introduces. B.3. Evaluation Dimensions Spatial understanding. This dimension includes one simple entry (fruit transfer), two intermediate entries (cloth folding and plate extraction), and two complex entries (test-tube transfer and mug hanging). Fruit transfer moves cherries, bananas, apples, oranges, and melons from bowls or plates into basket. Cloth folding varies size and orientation. Plate extraction requires one arm to lift bottle while the other removes and stacks the plate beneath it. Test-tube transfer and mug hanging further distinguish acquiring an object from completing the subsequent placement. Object generalization. The operation remains bottle handover or bowl stacking while the manipulated objects change. Handover introduces tea, coconut-water, and bottled-water containers, together with handled stainless-steel and plastic cups. Bowl stacking introduces stainless-steel bowls, small and large paper bowls, ceramic bowls, and large salad bowls. These variations probe differences in shape, size, material, and available grasp geometry. Instruction following. Three tests separate color, object, and spatial-language grounding. Color-conditioned cup stacking places two or three differently colored cups on the table and specifies which color should be stacked onto which other color. Object-conditioned pick-andplace uses toy car, five fruit types, blocks, and three tableware types, with bowls, plates, and baskets as target containers. Direction-conditioned bowl stacking requests left-to-right or right-to-left arrangements. These tests evaluate whether physically feasible operation is directed toward the requested object, destination, and spatial relation. Compositional generalization. Four entries recombine familiar operations, objects, and semantic constraints. Tissue extraction followed by disposal chains two actions into one objective. Stacking upward-facing cups changes the object configuration relative to the inverted-cup training template. Wiping whiteboard with rag combines the wiping operation with an object used elsewhere in the task catalogue, replacing the whiteboard eraser specified for training. Arranging cubes by color changes the criterion from the size ordering specified in the training catalogue. Together, these cases test action sequencing, object substitution, and semantic recombination. Unseen tasks. The final dimension organizes transfer by its relation to the training catalogue. Closing the microwave door isolates sub-action of the microwave loading routine. Taking bowl out of the microwave and unfolding rag reverse the corresponding loading and folding operations. Stacking books is listed as combined action, while building three-level Tower of Hanoi is listed as new action. 26 Table 3 Complete Real Eval test catalogue. Planning may reject command, or execution may stop making progress. Spatial Grounding Through Agent-Written Code Figure 15 Agent-written triangulation in insert_tubes. Matching pixels marked define viewing rays, illustrated schematically above the executed code excerpt. Recorded coordinates and reprojection errors connect the calculation to its output; the final frame follows subsequent grasping and insertion. The depth ablation in Section 5.1 raises practical question: how does an agent obtain usable spatial coordinates when its observations contain no depth? We examine two successful Qwen3.8-Flash-Next episodes from the no-depth, no-skill configuration. In both, the agent writes and executes geometry code using RGB observations and the supplied camera intrinsics and extrinsics, rather than calling the built-in triangulation operation. The cases illustrate different ways of constructing localization estimates: matching features across views and testing geometric assumptions against image evidence. E.1. Recovering Tube Positions Across Views In insert_tubes, the agent must place three tubes into rack. After obtaining image-space segmentation boxes, it captures additional camera views and writes Python function to intersect viewing rays in least-squares sense. It then selects corresponding tube-cap pixels and computes their world coordinates. Figure 15 follows one cap: the calculated position reprojects within 0.46 and 1.94 pixels of the selected points in the two views. This gives the agent way to check whether its chosen correspondences agree geometrically. The cap positions are only the beginning of the manipulation sequence. The agent subsequently estimates tube axes, chooses grasp poses, and uses observations and action feedback to guide lifting and insertion. The episode ends with all three tubes in the rack. Here, code execution turns image correspondences into coordinates that the agent can inspect and use in its action planning. 32 Figure 16 Geometric hypothesis testing in cover_blocks. The agent varies candidate table height and computes cup dimensions from selected pixels. The schematic illustrates the rayplane intersections computed by hit() in the code excerpt; the right-hand frame shows later placement over the red block. E.2. Exploring Geometry Before Moving Cup In cover_blocks, the agent must cover three colored blocks from left to right, then uncover them in specified color order. Locating the cups requires reasoning about their extent as well as their image centers. The agent extracts colored image regions and writes code that tests candidate table heights, intersects pixel rays with each candidate plane, and compares the resulting cup dimensions (Figure 16). The height sweep exposes how an assumed scene parameter changes the inferred geometry, rather than treating single image estimate as fixed. The agent continues by projecting candidate object shapes into the images and refining its scene estimates. It then uses the estimated cup positions to approach, grasp, and place the cups, checking the scene as the task proceeds. The recorded episode completes the required covering and uncovering sequence. This case shows more exploratory use of code: the agent constructs and tests geometric hypotheses before committing to physical actions. Together, the two cases illustrate how RGB-based localization can support successful execution, while requiring correspondence selection, geometric assumptions, and verification that depth access can simplify. F. Planning During Physical Execution The overlap measurements in Section 6.2 show when model requests and physical actions run concurrently, but not what the agent prepares during that time or how it uses the result. We follow longer excerpts from two recorded trajectories to connect this preparation to subsequent actions and feedback. Each figure pairs key observations with the recorded execution timeline and enlarges one interval in which the model generates concrete calculation while physical tool is running. The annotations summarize recorded outputs; the bars denote model requests, not measurement of internal reasoning time. Figure 17 Grasp adjustment and supported sliding in align_blocks. The upper row summarizes four stages, each illustrated by representative observation; stage may contain multiple tool calls. Green and blue bars show physical tools and model requests; shading marks overlap. The marked interval is enlarged below, where the model prepares clearance check during release. Image timestamps and the main axis are relative to the first displayed observation. F.1. From Regrasping to Supported Sliding In align_blocks, the agent must align three blocks with set square while keeping the blocks on the table. Figure 17 follows the trajectory from an uncertain grasp through contact adjustments to the final aligned row. While background release opens the gripper, the model generates Python check for lower grasp pose. Using the finger geometry and table height, it checks that the proposed pose leaves clearance even after 2 mm uncertainty allowance. The program runs after the release finishes, and the agent then moves to the checked pose, grasps, and tests retention with short lift. The lift does not retain the set square. The agent explicitly changes its approach: it will keep the square supported and use sliding contact instead. It lowers the hand, closes the gripper, and issues sequence of small rotations and translations, then inspects the scene and adjusts contact again. The final observation shows the blocks in row with the arms clear. This longer sequence shows both the use of preparation during background execution and the need to revise that preparation when subsequent physical evidence contradicts it. Figure 18 Orientation preparation during digit transport. The upper row summarizes four stages rather than individual tool calls; the lanes below show recorded execution. The enlarged interval shows model request preparing rotation candidates while transport continues. The later divergence is retained to show how execution feedback affects the prepared plan. Colors and time conventions match Figure 17. F.2. Preparing Reorientation During Transport In arrange_largest_number, the agent must place digit-shaped objects on pads to form the largest number. The excerpt in Figure 18 follows one digit from localization and grasping through transport and reorientation. While the arm moves toward raised target, the model generates program that composes candidate 90 and 180 world-axis rotations with the current orientation and converts them to Euler angles. This prepares later orientation commands without waiting for the transport result. The transport first exhausts its step budget, so the agent continues toward the same target before attempting the prepared rotation. The first orientation target is reached, but the next rotation stops for divergence. The agent then raises the hand while retaining its measured orientation and captures new observation. The sequence illustrates why advance preparation and execution monitoring are complementary: candidate action can be prepared during an earlier movement, while its application still depends on the state returned by the robot.
